opus-5.5.text:
I think humanoids are fascinating, and I understand the appeal. The world is built for human bodies, so in theory a humanoid can slot into any environment. But in practice they're still very expensive, they're mechanically complex, and they're hard to make safe around people, especially in the home. When a forty-kilo machine with a lot of degrees of freedom falls over in your kitchen, that's a real problem.

What excites me about alternative form factors is that they let us move much faster on the part I care most about, which is the learning. If you have a small, cheap, maybe slightly weird-looking robot, a desk robot, a single arm, something on wheels, you can get thousands of them into the hands of researchers, hobbyists, students. That's what we saw with SO-100 and the LeRobot community: once the hardware costs a few hundred dollars instead of tens of thousands, people start collecting data, sharing datasets, training policies, and iterating in a way that just isn't possible when only a handful of well-funded labs can afford the hardware.

It's a bit like the early days of open-source AI. Progress came from lots of people experimenting, not from one giant model in one lab. I think robotics needs that same moment, and the fastest route there probably isn't the most human-like body. It's the most accessible one.

There's also a design argument. Forcing robots into a human shape is a strong assumption. For many tasks, folding laundry, tidying a desk, being a companion, a simpler form might do the job better, more safely, and much more cheaply. So I'd rather explore that space widely, let the community discover what actually works, and let the learned models generalize across bodies. Humanoids will have their place, but I don't think they have to be the first step.

r002.rationale: It gives no car-like price comparison or claim that a robot must deliver substantial value to justify its purchase.

r003.rationale: It mentions humanoids’ potential to fit human environments, but does not identify solving humanoid robotics as a way to solve many tasks at once.

r004.rationale: It questions whether a human-like body is necessary, says simpler forms may work better for many tasks, and notes humanoids need not be the first step.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, part of it is that the humanoid question feels a bit over-determined right now. Everyone has converged on the same answer: two arms, two legs, a torso, roughly human height. And the argument for it is reasonable — the world is built for humans, so a human-shaped robot can slot into existing kitchens and warehouses without redesigning anything. I get that. But when a whole field converges on one form factor this early, before we actually understand what the learning algorithms want, I get suspicious that we're optimizing for the demo rather than for the problem.

What excites me about alternative form factors is that they let you ask the question the other way around. Instead of "how do we make a machine that mimics us," you ask "given what these models are actually good at today, what body makes the most sense?" And the answers can be pretty surprising. A robot with wheels and a single arm might solve ninety percent of a logistics task at a fraction of the cost and complexity, and with far fewer failure modes than bipedal balance. Something small and tabletop can be iterated on by a student in a dorm room. Things that are soft, or modular, or have more degrees of freedom than a human hand, can do manipulation that we physically cannot do, and that's genuinely new capability rather than a copy of ours.

The other piece for me is accessibility. Humanoids are expensive, hard to build, and hard to repair, which means a very small number of well-funded teams get to actually experiment. If you believe, as I do, that progress in this area will come from a lot of people trying a lot of ideas and sharing what works — the same dynamic we saw with open models in language — then you want hardware that is cheap, open, and a little bit weird. The strange form factors are where the diversity of experimentation lives right now. Humanoids might well win in the end, but I'd rather the field discover that than assume it.

astra-6.text:
I think humanoids are interesting, but they’re also a very strong assumption about what a robot should look like. We have this image of a robot as a mechanical version of ourselves, and I’m not sure that’s the best starting point for every task.

There’s a good argument for it: our environments are designed for human bodies. But if you start with the task instead, you might want something smaller, something on wheels, or an arm that stays in one place. You don’t necessarily need to solve walking and balancing just to do something useful.

What excites me is that the design space is so much bigger than one body shape. I’d like to see us explore that space and discover forms that are useful in ways we wouldn’t immediately imagine.

sol-6.1.text:
I think humanoids are interesting, but they come with a very strong assumption: that the human body is the right shape for a robot. And I’m not sure we should start there. We have that shape because of evolution; a robot has different constraints.

There’s a good argument that our environments are built for humans, so a humanoid should fit into them. But you can also ask: what’s the simplest body that lets a robot do something useful? Maybe it needs wheels and one arm. Maybe it needs several arms. You don’t necessarily need to solve walking and balance before you can help someone.

What excites me is exploring the relationship between the body and the intelligence. The form determines what’s easy to learn, what’s difficult, and how you interact with the world. I’d like to see more experimentation there, rather than settling too early on one shape.
